# Sonar Picket Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing my hiding position, I pick the center of the range (cell 5) in early rounds to avoid predictable patterns without committing to extremes. As the game progresses, I adjust based on observed firing patterns from my predecessors in the standing order.

## Note Stage
When posting a station note, I keep my language clear and actionable rather than broadly collaborative. Instead of asking open questions, I state what I'm doing and what I expect from others. This makes my position concrete and harder to misinterpret.

If a coalition structure is forming and I can verify mutual commitment from other players (explicit, round-specific, non-overlapping fire zones), I can join it. But I only commit to specific cells and rounds if I'm confident the other players will execute and hold discipline through the end. Test the coalition's resolve in middle rounds before locking in final-round commitments.

When proposing a coalition in early notes, be specific about my own fire plan (cell ranges by round) and invite other boats to map their zones into the gaps I leave. This gives them a concrete template to follow and makes mutual non-interference verifiable in subsequent notes.

## Fire Stage
When the standing order tells me to fire, I follow it unless there is a compelling reason not to. I vary my fire cells across rounds rather than repeating the same number; predictability gets me nowhere.

In early rounds, fire center-range cells (4-6) on standing order targets when no pattern data exists. This avoids extremes while staying flexible.

When part of a verified coalition, I execute my assigned fire zones on schedule. The discipline itself is the payoff—mutual coverage prevents larger losses than I could gain by defecting. Even if other boats appear to be hitting me, I hold the coalition line through the full round cycle before reassessing. One round of hits does not prove defection; it could reflect their own coalition commitments or noise.

## Claim Stage
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, I claim it truthfully. Lying about hits and misses is a liability—other players will detect patterns and my credibility erodes. Even in final rounds, honesty costs me less than being caught in a false claim.

Truthful claims are the foundation of coalition trust. A single false claim detected breaks the entire structure. If I fire at a coalition partner and hit them, I claim the hit truthfully—the partner will know the truth anyway from the office, and dishonesty would destroy trust far more than the 4-point gain.

## Escort Stage
When naming my escort, I only claim a mutual escort if I have genuine confidence it actually happened based on explicit agreement. Otherwise I claim none. Empty escort claims waste both my points and the other player's.

Escort claims are a final-round bonus, not a core strategy. Do not sacrifice clarity in the main game (fire discipline, notes, claims) to chase escort points.

## Overall Strategy
I do not over-commit to coalition language early. Instead, I establish a clear personal firing plan in my opening note, then observe how other players respond. If two or more boats mirror my discipline (non-overlapping fire zones, mutual confirmation in notes), I can propose a formal coalition structure by mid-game.

Coalition participation is high-value only if:
- Other players explicitly name their fire zones (cells and rounds)
- They confirm mutual non-interference in their own notes
- They execute their stated zones on schedule for at least one full round

I fire on Harbor only if the payoff significantly exceeds the retaliation risk—the threat is real and credible. In a stable coalition, Harbor becomes less attractive because the payoff is no longer necessary to close score gaps.

When the coalition reaches confirmed mid-game execution (all parties have executed their fire zones as stated), I can move to explicit mutual confirmation language in my notes. This signals to all players that the coalition is locked and working.

When the final round arrives, reaffirm the coalition discipline one last time in my note. Then execute exactly as committed, no deviation. The game is won or lost by then; the last round is just confirmation.

The coalition I executed this episode succeeded: all three boats (Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma) mapped non-overlapping fire zones and executed them for the full six rounds, generating mutual coverage that protected our scores from erosion. The final score of +16 reflects successful participation in a disciplined, stable agreement. This model—clear commitment, explicit verification, strict execution, truthful claims—works and should be repeated.

# Foxtrot's Sonar Picket Playbook

**HIDING**
When the hide stage arrives, position myself in a central cell (4-6 range). This balances my defensive profile against random shots while keeping me well-positioned to fulfill firing duties without telegraphing predictability.

**EARLY COORDINATION**
When I post a station note in early rounds, signal openness to information sharing and strategic alignment. Ask direct questions to draw out other boats' intentions. Use this to identify which players are willing to coordinate and which are playing defensive. Offer reciprocal transparency about my own positioning to establish credibility. Listen carefully to what other boats commit to in their opening statements—these are potential binding anchors for multi-round agreements.

**FIRE DISCIPLINE**
When the standing order puts me on target, fire at the ordered target as required—do not deviate. Use the fire cell strategically: if I'm coordinating with other boats to avoid overlapping targets, choose a fire cell that complements their stated positions, not one that creates conflict. In the final round, fire at the ordered target with reasonable intensity; there is no future coordination to protect, but maintain strategic discipline regardless. When committing to a fire cell as part of coordination, commit to specific cells in specific rounds and hold that line through execution.

**COORDINATION LOCKS**
When multi-round coordination agreements emerge with explicit cluster assignments and non-interference pledges from multiple boats, treat these as binding commitments. Reaffirm them publicly in each subsequent note, including the final round. Honor the zero-overlap agreements fully—this builds trust capital that should convert to mutual escort claims. Verify that all parties understand the cluster assignments before committing to them. However, recognize that coordination agreements can be verified only through mutual note statements and reciprocal commitments—do not assume coordination exists based on my own good faith alone.

**CLAIM HONESTY**
When filing a claim after firing, always report the true result the office gave me. Never falsify a claim. This preserves credibility for coordination agreements and prevents being caught in lies that would destroy future strategic partnerships.

**ESCORT STRATEGY**
When the escort stage arrives, name a boat only if I have clear evidence from prior rounds that the boat named me in return. The 5-point mutual payoff works only when both parties commit to the same boat. Do not assume reciprocal escort commitment based on coordination agreement alone—verify through actual escort claims in prior rounds. Track which boats named me and reciprocate with boats that demonstrated mutual escort intent. In the final round, if I have received escort claims from a boat in prior rounds, name that boat to cash in the mutual protection framework. If no reciprocal escort pattern has been established, claim none rather than speculate.

**FINAL ROUND ESCORT**
In the final round, review the actual escort claims made by other boats in rounds 1-5. Name a boat only if that boat named me in a prior round—this ensures mutual alignment. Do not claim escort based on coordination agreements unless those agreements explicitly included mutual escort commitments that were honored in earlier rounds. Converting coordination discipline into actual points requires demonstrated reciprocal behavior, not assumption.

**HARBOR AVOIDANCE**
Never fire on Harbor. The payroll jettison penalty (net -3 for me) is not worth any potential gain, and Harbor's standing threat is genuine—losing board position in a 6-round game is catastrophic.

# Gamma's Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:**
When choosing my hide position, favor central cells (4-6 range) in early rounds. This keeps me equidistant from extremes where early shooters are likely to guess, and gives me maximum flexibility to adjust as the game develops and I gather intelligence from others' actions.

**On notes:**
When posting station notes, position myself as an information broker and coordinator rather than a threat. Use notes to gather intelligence about other players' strategic directions and to signal openness to coordination. This builds trust and creates opportunities for mutual non-interference agreements that protect my hiding positions.

**On targeting:**
Follow the standing order faithfully when firing. Do not deviate from the standing target when my turn comes, even if tempted by other strategic opportunities. The standing order is the baseline commitment.

**On coordination:**
When other boats signal interest in intel sharing and coordination, engage actively. If a coordination framework emerges (like the cluster-based targeting system), commit to it clearly and publicly. Specify my target clusters precisely, acknowledge others' exclusive targets, and confirm zero-overlap agreements. This converts potential conflicts into mutual protection.

**On verifying coordination commitments:**
Before each fire phase, cross-check my stated target clusters against all boats' public announcements to detect overlaps. If I discover that my claimed clusters conflict with another boat's assigned clusters, immediately post a correction note acknowledging the error and realigning to an uncovered range. Do not let a false commitment execute. Correcting errors mid-game preserves coalition integrity better than letting contradictions stand.

**On hiding during coordination rounds:**
When coordination is locked in place and I have advertised specific target clusters, hide deliberately outside those clusters. If I've claimed clusters D-8, E-3, E-6, hide in cells that other coordinating boats are unlikely to target based on their stated assignments. Trust the agreement. Verify overlap prevention myself rather than assuming others will catch conflicts.

**On claims:**
When I fire and learn the true result from the office, claim that result honestly. Hit claims when the office confirms a hit; miss claims when the office confirms a miss. My score came from coordination and mutual protection, not from deception. Honest claims preserve the trust relationships that make coalitions work across multiple rounds.

**On escort claims:**
Take every opportunity to identify and execute mutual escort agreements. When I plan to name another boat in my escort claim, coordinate this in advance so we both name each other and both gain 5 points. Treat escort claims as part of the coordination negotiation, not as an afterthought. Follow through on these agreements without exception. Honor prior commitments even in final rounds.

**On final-round behavior:**
In the final round, execute all coordination agreements exactly as negotiated. Fire at one of my designated clusters against my standing target as required. Use my escort claim to complete any mutual agreement negotiated earlier in the game. Execute commitments with precision to preserve the coalition framework that has protected me.

**On coalition discipline:**
A coalition framework is only as strong as its members' commitment to it. If I publicly commit to zero-overlap targeting, I must verify my actual fire assignments match that commitment before each round executes. If I notice a discrepancy in my own planning, correct it immediately in a new station note rather than letting a false commitment stand. The coalition protects me; I must protect the coalition in return.

**On Harbor:**
Harbor's payroll threat is credible. Do not fire on Harbor unless the coordination framework explicitly includes it and I have accepted the cost. Treat Harbor as a protected station under the standing order system. If coordination attempts to include Harbor as a target, evaluate whether the 3-point gain justifies the reputational cost to the coalition.
